claims.text: A uniform local distribution of Al, Cr, and Si promotes formation of a continuous, adherent passivating oxide layer in high-temperature MPEAs.
A continuous and uniform oxide cap limits oxygen ingress and helps maintain material integrity.
Chemical segregation disrupts oxide-scale coherence and accelerates oxidation.
High-energy milling and extended homogenization heat treatments can enhance chemical homogeneity in an MPEA.
Tailored thermal treatments can induce microsegregation of passivating elements.
The relevant structural mediator is the continuity and adherence of a surface layer composed primarily of Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3.
A homogeneous elemental distribution makes oxidation-resistant elements uniformly accessible for nucleation of a protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer formed on a homogeneous alloy self-heals during high-temperature exposure.
Microsegregation creates local regions deficient in oxidation-resistant elements.
Local depletion of oxidation-resistant elements causes discontinuous oxide growth and increased oxygen diffusion into the substrate.
Discontinuous oxide growth and increased oxygen ingress ultimately accelerate material degradation.
Homogenized alloys will have lower oxidation rates than compositionally segregated alloys.
Homogenized alloys will form a more uniform and thicker passivating oxide layer than segregated alloys.
Homogenized alloys will experience delayed mechanical-property degradation relative to segregated alloys.
A conventionally processed baseline MPEA will show oxidation and degradation behavior intermediate between the homogenized and segregated samples.
The proposed governing behavior should apply between approximately 900 and 1100 °C in oxygen-rich environments.
Outside 900–1100 °C or in non-oxidative atmospheres, mechanisms other than oxide-scale continuity may govern degradation.
Minor alloying variations and secondary-phase formation may compete with the proposed homogeneity-controlled mechanism.
Similar scale coherence, oxidation rates, and mechanical degradation in homogeneous and segregated samples would falsify the proposed governing role of chemical homogeneity.
